title: Terra.do Climate Fellowship 2026: Apply for the 12-Week Climate Change Learning for Action Programme
summary: Are you looking to build a career in climate action, deepen your understanding of climate change, or transition your existing professional skills into the rapidly growing climate sector? The Terra.do Climate Fellowship: Climate Change – Learning for Action offers a structured 12-week learning experience designed to help participants understand the complexities of climate change, explore practical solutions and identify where their skills can make the greatest contribution to climate action. The fellowship brings together a global community of climate professionals, researchers, entrepreneurs, advocates, educators, sustainability specialists, technologists and other professionals interested in addressing climate challenges. The programme combines expert-led learning, practical projects, discussions, mentorship, career development and networking to help participants move from understanding climate problems to taking meaningful action. According to Terra.do, the fellowship has supported more than 7,000 graduates across more than 96 countries, with an average course rating of 9.3 and a reported career transition rate of more than 60 percent. About the Terra.do Climate Fellowship The Climate Change: Learning for Action fellowship is an expert-guided programme focused on helping participants understand climate science, climate impacts, policy, economics, technology, finance, sustainability and practical climate solutions. The programme is designed around the idea that climate action requires people from different professional backgrounds and disciplines. Participants therefore have an opportunity to explore the connections between science, business, policy, technology, communications, finance, agriculture and social change. Terra.do describes the programme as a journey that helps participants understand the climate problem while identifying practical solutions and finding a meaningful role within the climate sector. Key Features of the Climate Fellowship The fellowship is delivered entirely online and is structured to accommodate professionals and other participants who may have existing work or personal commitments. Key programme features include 100% online learning. Approximately 6 to 10 hours of study and participation each week. Between 10 and 12 expert lectures. Weekly deep dives and discussion groups. Hands-on projects. Personalised feedback and support. Tailored career development support. A digital certificate upon graduation. The programme also provides access to more than 100 updated learning modules covering a broad range of climate-related subjects. What Will Participants Learn? The curriculum explores climate change from scientific, economic, political, technological, social and professional perspectives. Major subject areas include: Climate science – Understanding the scientific foundations of climate change and the processes driving global warming. Climate impacts—Examining local and global consequences of climate change and how warming affects ecosystems, societies and economies. Energy – Exploring energy systems and the transition towards cleaner and more sustainable energy. Food and agriculture – Understanding the relationship between climate change, food systems and agriculture. Carbon removal – Examining approaches to removing carbon dioxide from the atmosphere. Climate politics—Exploring policy choices, governance and political approaches to climate action. Climate economics – Understanding the economic dimensions of climate change, including markets, costs and policy interventions. Climate communications – Learning how climate issues can be communicated effectively to different audiences. Climate finance – Exploring the role of financial systems and investment in addressing climate change. Climate risk – Understanding climate-related risks and their implications for organisations and communities. Corporate sustainability—Examining how organisations can incorporate climate considerations into business strategies. Adaptation – Exploring approaches for preparing communities and systems for the impacts of climate change. Alternative development models – Considering different approaches to economic and social development in the context of environmental sustainability. Expert-Led Climate Learning The fellowship brings together educators, scientists, entrepreneurs, lawyers, journalists, policy specialists and other practitioners working on climate solutions. The programme explains that climate action is shaped by multiple perspectives, including science, policy, technology and justice. Participants therefore have opportunities to learn from people actively working on climate challenges rather than relying exclusively on theoretical material. The programme has featured professionals such as clean-technology entrepreneur Danny Kennedy, climate scientist Dr. Zachary Labe, Stanford professor Mark Z. Jacobson and environmental lawyer Melissa Hornbein. Other experts highlighted by the programme include climate journalist David Roberts, Dr. Tracey Osborne, renewable-energy entrepreneur Dr. Jeremy Leggett, Jamie Alexander and Goldman Environmental Prize winner Kimiko Hirata. A Curriculum Designed for a Changing Climate Sector Climate science, technology, markets and policies are constantly evolving. The fellowship therefore states that its curriculum is regularly refreshed with new case studies, developments, tools and frameworks. Participants are exposed to current approaches and emerging developments designed to help them understand both the technical and human dimensions of climate solutions. This makes the programme relevant to professionals who want to understand not only the fundamentals of climate change but also how the climate sector is evolving. Climate Fellowship Syllabus and Weekly Structure The programme consists of 20 classes and more than 100 modules, supported by expert-led lectures and workshops, discussions, career support, networking and individual feedback. The syllabus begins with the fundamentals before progressing into more complex areas of climate solutions. Week 1: Introduction to Climate Change Participants begin by examining the fundamentals of climate change. Topics include: Building a simple climate model. The greenhouse effect. Radiative and climate forcing. Drivers of climate change. Week 2: Foundations of Climate Science The second week focuses on emissions and the global carbon cycle. Participants explore: The global carbon cycle. Global warming potential. Methane and other greenhouse gases. Emissions accounting. Week 3: Climate Impacts and Personal Resilience This stage examines the consequences of a changing climate, including: The significance of the 1.5°C target. When warming could stop. Changes in temperature and rainfall. Ice and sea-level changes. Ocean currents. The global carbon budget. Week 4: Climate Solutions and Communication Participants explore different approaches to addressing climate change and learn how to compare solutions based on factors such as impact and cost. The week also introduces mental models and different ways of framing climate issues. Week 5: Climate Economics, Politics and Justice The programme then examines the economic and political dimensions of climate change. Topics include: Climate change as a market failure. Alternative approaches to environmental economics. Climate policy options. Carbon pricing. Carbon markets. The social cost of carbon. Week 6: Systems Thinking and Energy Participants are introduced to systems thinking in relation to climate mitigation and the importance of energy. The programme includes an En-ROADS workshop by Climate Interactive , facilitated by a Climate Interactive ambassador. The supplied programme information displays the first six weeks of the syllabus in detail, while indicating that the wider curriculum continues beyond these modules. Weekly Learning Schedule The fellowship uses a combination of asynchronous learning, optional career sessions, expert deep dives, guest talks, live laboratories and networking activities. A typical week includes: Sunday: Asynchronous classes are released. Monday: Optional careers session. Tuesday: Optional deep-dive session. Wednesday: Guest talk. Thursday: Live laboratory. Friday: Optional networking and co-working session. The programme recognises that fellows may have work or family responsibilities. Mandatory sessions are recorded and can be watched asynchronously when participants are unable to attend live. Hands-On Projects and Practical Learning The fellowship goes beyond lectures by providing real-world assignments and projects. Participants work on individual and team projects designed to help them: Apply climate knowledge to their local context. Develop their climate voice. Build a portfolio of climate-related work. Strengthen communication skills. Improve collaboration skills. This practical component can be particularly useful for professionals who want to demonstrate their climate knowledge and experience when pursuing future opportunities. Personalised Feedback and Instruction Participants receive individualised support throughout the programme. The fellowship states that instructors track participants progress and provide the following: One-on-one support. Individual feedback on assignments. Personalised career-transition advice. Participants can also book one-on-one sessions to discuss their climate learning and career journey. Climate Lab Groups Participants meet weekly in small groups with instructors for interactive learning. These sessions include: Discussions around the week s topics. Presentations by fellow learners. Action-oriented and creative group activities. The group-based structure allows participants to learn from people with different professional backgrounds and perspectives. Career Development and Climate Job Support One of the central features of the fellowship is its focus on career development. Terra.do state that thousands of alumni have transitioned into roles across climate technology, policy, advocacy and other areas. Following completion of the programme, fellows can access a climate career coach who can help them: Determine how to enter the climate sector if they have limited previous experience. Identify climate jobs that match their existing skills. Develop a job-search strategy. Build a networking strategy. Accelerate their career transition. The programme therefore provides a pathway for participants who are not necessarily starting their careers in climate but want to transfer existing professional skills into the sector. Global Climate Mentorship Participants can also access guidance from experienced professionals working across different climate sectors. The programme highlights: More than 200 mentors. Mentors across more than 20 countries. Carefully curated climate experts. Mentorship across energy, policy, agriculture, sustainability, ESG, climate finance and other sectors. One-on-one time for personalised career guidance. This international mentorship component can help participants better understand career pathways and professional opportunities across the climate economy. Who Is the Climate Fellowship Designed For? The programme is not limited to one professional discipline. Instead, it is designed for people with different skills and backgrounds who want to contribute to climate solutions. Advocacy and Policy Professionals The fellowship is suitable for professionals interested in climate policy, adaptation, resilience, climate justice and strengthening climate-related work within government or non-governmental organisations. Business Professionals People working in sales, marketing, business development, finance and related functions can use the programme to explore climate career transitions or contribute to corporate climate leadership. Technologists Engineers, data scientists and product managers interested in climate technology, climate startups and technology-enabled climate solutions are also identified as potential participants. Climate Scientists Researchers, analysts and scientists working in academic, government or private-sector settings can use the programme to connect their expertise with real-world climate challenges. Sustainability Consultants Professionals working in sustainability consulting, corporate ESG strategy and environmental impact assessment can benefit from the programme s focus on systemic climate action. Community Organisers and Educators Grassroots activists, educators and nonprofit leaders working on public awareness, community mobilisation, climate justice and policy advocacy are also among the audiences identified by the programme. Global Eligibility and Geographic Reach The supplied programme information presents the fellowship as a global programme. Terra.do reports graduates from more than 96 countries, indicating a broad international community. However, the source does not provide a formal list of eligible nationalities, countries, races or continents, nor does it identify a race or ethnicity requirement. Prospective applicants should therefore consult the official application process for any eligibility conditions that may apply to the specific cohort. What Can Participants Gain From the Fellowship? The programme is structured to provide a combination of climate knowledge, practical experience, professional development and community. Key areas of value include: A structured understanding of climate science and climate solutions. Exposure to climate policy and economics. Knowledge of energy, agriculture, carbon removal and adaptation. Understanding of climate finance and climate risk. Practical project experience. Individual feedback from instructors. Career transition guidance. Access to climate mentors. Networking with an international community. Opportunities to learn from climate practitioners. A digital certificate upon graduation. Alumni Career Outcomes Terra.do highlights alumni who have moved into different climate-related roles and organisations. Examples provided on the programme page include transitions into executive assistance, programme management, commercial leadership, environmental project leadership, technical specialist positions and other climate-related roles. The programme also states that more than 200 fellows are now running climate startups across different sectors. In addition, more than 500 fellows are described as advancing climate and sustainability objectives within their organisations. Open House and Alumni Engagement Prospective applicants can also engage with alumni and instructors through open house sessions. These sessions provide opportunities to: Meet and interact with alumni. Learn more about the programme. Ask questions directly to instructors. Gain insights into the fellowship experience. Applicants who want more personalised guidance can also schedule a one-on-one discussion about the programme and potential climate career pathways. Fellowship Cost and Scholarship Information The listed course fee for the programme is US$1,990 . The programme states that applicants can pay the fee in instalments and that there is a three-week money-back guarantee for participants who are not satisfied within the specified period. The source also states that journalists may be eligible for scholarships of up to 80% , depending on their application. The supplied page also displays a scholarship invitation associated with the applicant s referral context. Prospective applicants should therefore check the application page to determine what scholarship or funding options are available to them. Application Process The stated application process is designed to be relatively straightforward. Step 1: Submit Your Application Applicants are asked to explain their motivation for joining the programme and can request scholarship support if they need financial assistance. Step 2: Admission and Scholarship Decision Terra.do states that applications are reviewed within 24 hours and that applicants are notified of admission and scholarship decisions. Step 3: Complete Payment and Enrol Successful applicants can pay the programme fee either in full or through instalments and secure their place in the upcoming cohort. Application Deadline and Cohort Start Date The application deadline is September 22 , while the upcoming cohort is scheduled to begin on September 28 . Applicants interested in joining the programme should submit their applications before the stated deadline and review the official application requirements before applying. How to Apply for the Terra.do Climate Fellowship Interested applicants can apply through the official Terra.do programme page. Before submitting an application, prospective fellows should carefully review the programme structure, syllabus, financial requirements, scholarship information and application conditions. APPLY HERE Why Consider the Climate Change: Learning for Action Fellowship? Climate change affects virtually every major sector of society, from energy and agriculture to finance, infrastructure, business, health, development and public policy. As organisations increasingly need professionals who understand climate risks and solutions, gaining structured knowledge of climate action can help professionals identify new areas where their existing skills can be applied. The Terra.do fellowship brings together scientific learning, practical projects, expert instruction, mentorship and career development within one programme. Its international community also gives participants an opportunity to learn alongside people approaching climate challenges from different professional and geographical perspectives. For professionals seeking to transition into climate work, researchers looking to connect their expertise with practical solutions, business professionals exploring climate leadership, or advocates and educators seeking stronger climate knowledge, the programme provides a structured environment for learning and professional development. Visit HERE for more information about the Terra.do Climate Fellowship 2026. Conclusion The Terra.do Climate Fellowship: Climate Change – Learning for Action is a 12-week online programme designed to help participants understand climate change and develop the knowledge, practical experience and professional connections needed to contribute to climate solutions. With more than 100 learning modules, expert-led lectures, weekly discussions, practical projects, personalised feedback, career support and access to an international network of climate professionals and mentors, the fellowship offers a multidisciplinary approach to climate education and career development. The programme is open to people from a wide range of professional backgrounds, including policy, business, technology, science, sustainability, community organising and education. The programme information indicates a global reach across more than 96 countries, although it does not specify a race, nationality or continent restriction. With the application deadline set for September 22 and the cohort scheduled to start on September 28 , interested applicants should review the programme carefully and submit their applications before the deadline. title: AARP Foundation California Quality Employment Grant 2026: Up to $750,000 for Projects Supporting Older Workers
summary: The AARP Foundation has announced a new grant opportunity aimed at improving access to quality employment for older adults with low incomes in California. Through its Request for Applications (RFA): Quality Employment for Older Workers in California , the Foundation intends to support projects that strengthen workforce systems, improve employment services, and create better pathways to stable and sustainable work for people aged 50 and above who experience financial insecurity. AARP Foundation plans to invest approximately $2 million in grant funding through this initiative and expects to support between four and eight organizations. Successful applicants may receive grants ranging from $250,000 to $750,000 , depending on the size, duration, activities, and expected outcomes of their proposed projects. The opportunity is particularly relevant to organizations, coalitions, workforce leaders, community organizations, and other eligible entities working to improve how workforce systems serve older workers. Rather than focusing primarily on conventional direct-service delivery, the RFA emphasizes systems change , age-inclusive workforce practices, improved coordination among services, and stronger pathways to quality employment. About the AARP Foundation California Quality Employment Grant The AARP Foundation is seeking innovative projects that can help make workforce systems more responsive to the needs of older adults with low incomes. Older workers can encounter significant challenges when seeking employment, remaining in work, changing careers, or re-entering the workforce after unemployment. These challenges can include age-related barriers in recruitment, limited access to relevant training, difficulty navigating employment and public-benefit systems, and a lack of coordinated support during periods of job transition. Through this funding opportunity, AARP Foundation wants to support approaches that address these structural and systemic challenges. The Foundation is particularly interested in projects that incorporate age-inclusive practices into workforce systems and services and create stronger pathways toward quality employment for adults aged 50 and above. What Does AARP Foundation Mean by Quality Employment? For this grant opportunity, quality employment goes beyond simply helping someone find a job. A quality job should provide conditions that allow an individual to achieve greater financial stability while developing the skills and support necessary to remain employed and progress professionally. According to the grant description, quality employment includes work that provides: Stable earnings. Fair and equitable treatment. Opportunities to develop skills. Opportunities for advancement. Flexibility that helps workers remain employed. Appropriate support during employment transitions. Conditions that contribute to longer-term employment sustainability. This means applicants should think beyond traditional job-placement activities. Strong proposals should demonstrate how their interventions can help improve the broader systems, structures, and services that determine whether older workers can access and maintain quality employment. Main Areas of Interest AARP Foundation has identified two major areas that applicants may address through their proposed projects. 1. Age-Inclusive Training, Education, and Employment Services The first area focuses on improving workforce training, education, and employment services so that they intentionally respond to the needs of older workers. Many existing workforce programs are designed for broad populations and may not adequately account for the circumstances faced by adults aged 50 and above. AARP Foundation is therefore interested in approaches that redesign or improve these programs to make them more age-inclusive. Potential activities may include: Redesigning job-connected training programs to intentionally serve older workers. Modifying workforce services to better address the needs of adults aged 50 and above. Developing new approaches for reaching older workers who may not be adequately served by existing employment systems. Creating recruitment strategies specifically designed to engage older workers. Helping older adults prepare for quality employment opportunities. Connecting older workers with employers offering suitable employment opportunities. Improving the ability of workforce organizations to identify and respond to barriers experienced by older job seekers. Developing employment pathways that recognize the experience, skills, and needs of older workers. Applicants should demonstrate how their proposed intervention could improve the effectiveness or inclusiveness of existing workforce systems rather than simply providing temporary assistance to individual participants. 2. Age-Inclusive Workforce Systems and Service Alignment The second major area of interest focuses on improving coordination among workforce systems, public agencies, community organizations, and other support services. Older adults experiencing unemployment or employment transitions may need to interact with multiple systems at the same time. These can include workforce development services, unemployment support, employment agencies, community organizations, and public-benefit programs. When these systems operate independently, individuals may encounter fragmented services, duplicated processes, unclear referral pathways, or difficulty understanding where to obtain appropriate support. AARP Foundation is therefore interested in projects that strengthen connections between these systems. Potential approaches could include: Building stronger connections between unemployment services and workforce development programs. Improving coordination between reemployment services and other employment-support systems. Developing stronger referral pathways between public agencies and community-based organizations. Testing coordinated service models specifically designed to reach older workers. Improving how older adults navigate multiple benefits and support services. Creating partnerships among organizations serving older adults experiencing employment transitions. Developing systems that make it easier for older workers to move between workforce and support services. Testing approaches that can eventually be replicated or adopted more broadly. The Grant Is Focused on Systems Change One of the most important aspects of this opportunity is that applicants should understand the distinction between systems change and traditional direct service delivery. AARP Foundation specifically states that projects should focus on systems change initiatives rather than direct service programs . This means an applicant should not simply propose to provide employment services directly to a group of older adults without explaining how the project will change, improve, coordinate, or strengthen the systems through which those services are delivered. For example, a conventional direct-service project might focus primarily on helping a specific number of individuals prepare résumés or find jobs. A systems-change project, by contrast, could examine how workforce organizations identify older job seekers, redesign their service models, improve referral systems, coordinate with community organizations, or change workforce practices so that older workers can consistently receive better support. Applicants should therefore clearly demonstrate the broader structural impact their project could have. Who Should Benefit From the Project? The proposed projects must primarily benefit older adults aged 50 and above with low incomes or financial insecurity . The target population is particularly important because the grant is designed around older workers who rely on employment to meet basic needs. Applicants should therefore demonstrate a clear understanding of the employment challenges faced by financially vulnerable older adults and explain how their proposed systems-level intervention will improve access to quality employment. A strong proposal should establish: Who the intended older-worker population is. What employment-related challenges this population experiences. Why existing systems and services are insufficient. What systemic barrier the project intends to address. How the proposed intervention will improve workforce systems. How the project will ultimately create better employment pathways. How success will be measured. Where Must Projects Be Implemented? The projects supported through this funding opportunity must be implemented in the state of California . This geographic requirement is central to the RFA. Applicants should ensure that their proposed activities, partnerships, workforce systems, and intended impact are connected to California. Organizations outside California should carefully review the complete RFA and FAQ before determining whether they are eligible to participate, particularly if they intend to partner with California-based organizations. The opportunity should not be interpreted as a general international or worldwide employment grant. Its stated purpose is to address quality employment for older adults with low incomes in California . How Much Funding Is Available? AARP Foundation expects to invest approximately $2 million through this grant opportunity. The Foundation anticipates making awards to up to four but no more than eight grantees . Individual grant awards are expected to range from: Minimum expected award: $250,000. Maximum expected award: $750,000. Applicants are expected to request an amount that is appropriate for the scope of their proposed project, activities, implementation period, and anticipated outcomes. The grant structure is designed to allow applicants to develop projects of different durations while matching their funding request to the scale of the intervention. Funding Based on Project Duration The maximum funding amount depends partly on the proposed implementation period. 12-Month Projects Projects proposed for a 12-month implementation period may request up to $375,000 . Applicants choosing this duration should ensure that the proposed activities and outcomes can realistically be achieved within one year. The project should have a clearly defined implementation strategy, measurable outcomes, and a realistic timeline demonstrating how the proposed systems change can occur during the funding period. 24-Month Projects Projects proposed for a 24-month implementation period may request up to $750,000 . A two-year project may provide greater opportunity to develop partnerships, test new approaches, implement systems changes, evaluate results, and refine interventions. However, a larger funding request should be supported by a clearly defined scope of work and a strong explanation of why the proposed activities require the requested level of investment. Important Proposal Considerations Organizations preparing an application should pay close attention to the central requirements of the RFA. Focus on Older Workers The proposed intervention must primarily affect adults aged 50 and above who have low incomes, experience financial insecurity, or depend on employment to meet basic needs. Demonstrate Systems-Level Impact The project should be designed to change or improve workforce systems rather than operate solely as a conventional direct-service program. Address Quality Employment Applicants should explain how their project will contribute to employment that offers stability, fair treatment, skill development, advancement opportunities, flexibility, and support. Establish California-Based Impact The project must be implemented in California, and the proposed activities should clearly demonstrate relevance to the state s workforce environment. Develop a Strong Partnership Strategy Because workforce systems involve multiple organizations and services, applicants should consider how collaboration, referrals, coordination, and service alignment can contribute to the proposed intervention. Connect Activities to Measurable Outcomes Applicants should explain what they intend to change and how they will determine whether the project has achieved its objectives. Rather than simply listing activities, the proposal should establish a logical connection between the identified problem, proposed intervention, expected outputs, and anticipated outcomes. Application Process The grant opportunity involves a two-stage application process . Stage One: Pre-Application Interested applicants must first submit a pre-application through AARP Foundation s grant portal. The pre-application is the initial screening stage of the funding process. Applicants should review the full RFA carefully before submitting their materials to ensure that the proposed project aligns with the Foundation s objectives, eligibility requirements, geographic restrictions, target population, and systems-change focus. The pre-application must be submitted through the AARP Foundation s Fluxx Grantee Portal . Stage Two: Full Application Following the review of pre-applications, selected applicants will be invited to submit a full application. According to the published schedule, invitations to submit full applications are expected around mid-September 2026 . The full application will provide shortlisted applicants with an opportunity to present their proposed project in greater detail. Organizations should therefore begin preparing their project concept, partnerships, implementation plan, expected outcomes, and budget before the invitation stage rather than waiting until the full application period begins. Key Dates and Deadlines Applicants should pay close attention to the following dates: Date Milestone August 6, 2026 Funding opportunity announced and pre-application made available Week of August 17, 2026 FAQ expected to become available September 1, 2026, at 7:00 p.m. PT / 10:00 p.m. ET Pre-application submission deadline Mid-September 2026 Selected applicants invited to submit full applications Mid-October 2026 Full application submission deadline October–November 2026 Clarification and follow-up period, as needed December 2026 Applicants notified of funding decisions Application Deadline The most immediate deadline is: September 1, 2026, at 7:00 p.m. Pacific Time / 10:00 p.m. Eastern Time. Applicants should avoid waiting until the final hours to submit their pre-application. Technical issues, incomplete information, or difficulties with the grant portal can create unnecessary risks close to the deadline. Where to Find the Full RFA The complete grant requirements, application instructions, eligibility information, and additional details are contained in AARP Foundation s official Request for Applications. Applicants should read the complete RFA rather than relying solely on summaries because the official document contains the detailed requirements governing the application. Questions and Technical Support Applicants who have questions about the RFA or require technical support with submitting an application through the AARP Foundation s Fluxx Grantee Portal can contact the AARP Foundation Grants Management team. Email: aarp_foundation_grants@aarp.org Questions relating to eligibility, proposal requirements, or technical submission issues should be addressed as early as possible so applicants have adequate time to resolve any concerns before the deadline. Frequently Asked Questions Can an individual apply for this grant? The opportunity is structured around projects led by eligible organizations, leaders, and coalitions rather than individual applicants seeking personal financial assistance. Potential applicants should consult the full RFA for the precise organizational eligibility requirements. Can organizations outside California apply? The RFA states that projects must be implemented in California . Organizations considering participation from outside the state should carefully review the full eligibility provisions and FAQ, particularly where partnerships with California-based organizations are involved. Can multiple organizations collaborate on a proposal? The RFA includes a question addressing proposals involving multiple partner organizations. Given the focus on workforce-system alignment, partnerships and collaboration may be particularly relevant to projects seeking to improve connections among public agencies, workforce organizations, community organizations, and support services. Applicants should consult the full RFA for the specific requirements governing collaborative proposals. What is the difference between quality employment and simply having a job? The grant opportunity takes a broader view of employment. Quality employment should provide stable earnings, fair treatment, opportunities for skills development and advancement, flexibility, and sufficient support to help workers sustain employment through subsequent transitions. Consequently, projects should demonstrate how their proposed systems changes can contribute to these broader employment outcomes. What does systems change mean in this opportunity? Systems change refers to interventions that alter or improve the way workforce systems, organizations, services, policies, processes, partnerships, or referral mechanisms operate. Applicants should therefore demonstrate how their project can produce changes that extend beyond providing temporary services directly to individual participants. How to Prepare a Competitive Application Organizations considering this opportunity can take several practical steps to strengthen their proposals. 1. Clearly Define the Problem Begin by identifying a specific workforce-system challenge affecting low-income older adults in California. Explain the problem using evidence, local knowledge, workforce data, organizational experience, or other credible information. 2. Identify the Systemic Barrier Do not stop at describing unemployment or financial insecurity. Explain why the existing workforce system is not adequately addressing the problem and identify the structural or organizational barrier that the project will address. 3. Demonstrate Age Inclusivity Explain how the proposed approach will intentionally address the circumstances and needs of workers aged 50 and above. The age-inclusive component should be central to the project rather than an incidental feature. 4. Build a Strong Theory of Change A strong proposal should demonstrate a logical progression: Problem → Systemic Barrier → Intervention → System Change → Improved Workforce Services → Better Employment Pathways → Improved Outcomes for Older Workers This makes it easier for reviewers to understand why the proposed project is likely to produce meaningful results. 5. Develop Meaningful Partnerships Consider which organizations influence the employment experiences of older workers. Potential partners could include workforce development organizations, public agencies, community organizations, employers, training institutions, and other relevant stakeholders. 6. Establish Measurable Outcomes Applicants should identify realistic indicators for determining whether the intervention is successful. Possible areas of measurement could include improvements in service coordination, referral effectiveness, workforce-system participation, employer engagement, access to training, or pathways to quality employment, depending on the proposed project. 7. Prepare a Realistic Budget The funding request should correspond with the scope and duration of the proposed intervention. A larger request should be supported by sufficient activities, staffing, partnerships, evaluation, and expected outcomes to justify the investment. 8. Review the Official RFA Carefully Finally, applicants should compare their proposed project against every requirement in the official RFA before submitting the pre-application. The official document should be treated as the authoritative source for eligibility and application requirements. APPLY HERE Why This Grant Opportunity Matters The transition into later working life can be financially challenging, particularly for people who have limited savings or depend on employment to meet essential needs. At the same time, older workers bring substantial experience, professional knowledge, technical skills, institutional understanding, and other valuable capabilities to the workforce. The challenge is therefore not simply getting older adults into employment. It is also ensuring that workforce systems recognize their needs and help them access jobs that provide stability, fair treatment, development opportunities, flexibility, and sustainable employment conditions. The AARP Foundation grant provides an opportunity to address these challenges at a broader systems level. Instead of funding only individual employment interventions, the initiative seeks to encourage changes in the systems and services that shape how older workers access employment opportunities. Visit HERE to learn more about the AARP Foundation California Quality Employment Grant 2026. Final Takeaway The AARP Foundation Quality Employment for Older Workers in California Grant 2026 represents a significant funding opportunity for eligible organizations and coalitions seeking to improve workforce systems for financially vulnerable adults aged 50 and above. With approximately $2 million available , individual awards expected to range from $250,000 to $750,000 , and project periods of 12 to 24 months , the opportunity can provide substantial resources for organizations developing ambitious systems-change initiatives. However, applicants should pay particular attention to three fundamental requirements: the project must primarily benefit older adults aged 50+ with low incomes or financial insecurity , it must be implemented in California , and it must focus on systems change rather than primarily delivering direct services . The immediate deadline is September 1, 2026, at 7:00 p.m. Pacific Time / 10:00 p.m. Eastern Time for the pre-application. Organizations that believe their work aligns with the Foundation s objectives should review the complete RFA, assess their eligibility, develop a clear systems-change strategy, establish appropriate partnerships, prepare a realistic funding request, and submit their pre-application through the official AARP Foundation grant portal before the deadline. title: We Are Not Waiting 2026: Young Changemakers Aged 14–35 Invited to Submit Abstracts for Global Youth-Led Systems Change Anthology
summary: We Are Not Waiting is a global youth-led initiative inviting young people who are already creating fairer, more sustainable and socially just futures to put their work on the record through an open-access anthology co-produced by The 50 Percent at the Club of Rome and the UNESCO–MOST BRIDGES UK Hub . The initiative is calling on young practitioners aged 14 to 35 who are actively working to transform communities and systems through areas such as regenerative economics, climate justice, circular living, peacebuilding, mutual aid, art, culture and storytelling. Rather than focusing only on theories about what a better future could look like, We Are Not Waiting seeks to document what young people are already doing in practice. Across communities worldwide, young people are organising, restoring ecosystems, developing alternative economic models, creating networks of solidarity, strengthening social cohesion, using creativity to challenge dominant narratives and finding new approaches to persistent social and environmental problems. Applicants do not need to be academics, professional researchers or established writers. The organisers are specifically interested in lived experience, practical action and original perspectives from young people who are actively engaged in the work they want to write about. Interested participants must submit an abstract of no more than 500 words by 31 August 2026 . Approximately 18 contributions are expected to form the final anthology. Applicants whose abstracts are selected will be invited to develop their ideas into full contributions of approximately 2,000 words , with editorial support provided throughout the writing process. The resulting open-access anthology will contain six chapters covering six major themes of systems change , with the project aiming to launch the publication at the UNESCO MOST Forum 2027 . About the We Are Not Waiting Initiative We Are Not Waiting : Amplifying Youth-Led Initiatives for Systems Change is designed around a simple but important idea: young people are not merely waiting for governments, institutions or established leaders to create solutions to the world s interconnected challenges. They are already building alternatives. The project centres young people aged 14–35 as designers and practitioners of alternative systems that are already in motion. It aims to showcase real-world initiatives and create a durable record of how youth-led systems change is happening in communities. The initiative has two major components: An open-access anthology comprising six chapters across six themes, with the aim of launching at the UNESCO MOST Forum 2027. A webinar series exploring the six themes through one question-and-answer session and two youth-led thematic sessions. At the heart of the project is the anthology, which is intended to be much more than a traditional collection of essays. It will serve as a policy-relevant record of youth-led systems change grounded in practical experiences. What Makes the We Are Not Waiting Anthology Different? The anthology is being deliberately designed to place young people s knowledge, experiences and perspectives at its centre. Three characteristics distinguish the publication: It is written, reviewed and edited by young people themselves. It is grounded in real-world practice rather than abstract discussion alone. It will be published in an open-access format , making the resulting knowledge accessible to a wider audience. The project provides young practitioners with an opportunity to document what they have learned through their initiatives while contributing to broader conversations about systemic change, social transformation and innovation. Who Can Submit an Abstract? The call is open to anyone aged 14 to 35 at the time of submission who is actively engaged in work connected to at least one of the anthology s six themes. Applicants do not need: Academic credentials; An institutional affiliation; To be professional researchers; To be established writers; or To have definitive solutions to the challenges they are addressing. Instead, the central requirement is that the proposed contribution must be grounded in genuine lived experience and real engagement with the issue or initiative being discussed . Applicants may submit either: Individually , or As part of a small team . For team submissions, all contributing authors must satisfy the 14–35 age requirement . The organisers particularly encourage contributions from the Global Majority and indigenous communities , helping ensure that perspectives and knowledge systems that may be underrepresented in conventional academic and policy discussions are included. Special Submission Requirement for Applicants Aged 18 and Under There is an additional submission procedure for younger participants. If an entrant is 18 years old or younger , their submission must be made on their behalf by an adult, such as: A parent; A guardian; or A teacher. The submission should include the young entrant s details together with the adult s contact information. This does not change the emphasis on the young person s ideas and experience; it is a procedural requirement for submitting the application. What Should You Submit? Applicants are invited to submit an abstract of no more than 500 words . The abstract should be written in the applicant s own voice using clear and accessible language. Academic or highly technical terminology is not required. The organisers want submissions that communicate real experiences and original thinking rather than attempting to sound like conventional academic papers. A strong abstract should address four key areas . 1. Describe Your Initiative, Project or Practice Explain the initiative, project, activity, network or practice that you want to write about. Applicants should provide enough context for reviewers to understand: What the work involves; Where or within what context it operates; What issue it seeks to address; Who is involved; and What the applicant s connection to the initiative is. 2. Explain What Makes the Work Distinct Applicants should explain what their work does differently. Consider questions such as: What conventional approach does the initiative challenge? What does the work refuse or seek to change? What alternative does it provide? How does the initiative rethink an existing system or practice? The objective is to demonstrate how the work contributes to creating or imagining different systems rather than merely reproducing existing approaches. 3. Ground the Contribution in Concrete Examples The anthology is focused on practice. Applicants should therefore show that their proposed full contribution will include real examples rather than relying exclusively on theoretical arguments. This could include experiences from communities, projects, campaigns, organisations, networks, cultural initiatives, environmental actions or other practical work. 4. Reflect on Learning and Broader Systems Change Applicants should also explain what they and their communities have learned through the work. The abstract should indicate how the initiative has contributed, or could contribute, to broader systemic change. The focus is therefore not simply on describing an activity but on examining what that activity reveals about how systems can be challenged, repaired, redesigned or transformed. Six Themes for the We Are Not Waiting Anthology Applicants must connect their abstract to one of six major themes. Theme 1: Re-weaving the Future — Networks and Economies That Make the World Anew This theme focuses on regenerative economics and community-centred alternatives to conventional economic systems. The organisers are interested in projects and practices demonstrating how young people are redesigning systems involving: Exchange; Value creation; Resource sharing; Community economies; Regenerative approaches; and Networks built around relationships and collective wellbeing. The emphasis is on a relational rather than merely technical approach to economic transformation. Young people who are experimenting with alternative economic systems, community-led resource models or regenerative approaches may find this theme particularly relevant. Theme 2: Building Resilience Through Ecological Resistance and Restoration This theme centres on climate justice, ecological resistance and environmental restoration . The organisers are seeking stories and experiences that demonstrate how young people are defending, restoring and renewing the living world. Relevant work may involve areas such as: Climate justice activism; Ecosystem restoration; Community environmental action; Ecological resistance; Biodiversity protection; Environmental justice; and Relationships between communities and ecosystems. The focus extends beyond simply managing environmental problems. Contributors are encouraged to reflect on what it means to actively defend and renew the living world . Theme 3: Living Circular Futures — Small Changes, Big Difference The third theme explores circular living and low-impact innovation . The organisers are particularly interested in concrete and practice-oriented examples showing how people can adapt their ways of living, producing, consuming and sharing resources. Contributions may explore change occurring at different levels, including: Personal practices; Community initiatives; Local innovation; Circular economic models; Low-impact approaches; and Broader systemic transformation. Applicants should demonstrate what circularity looks like when translated from an idea into real-world practice. Theme 4: Between Fracture and Repair — Youth-Led Peacebuilding and Social Cohesion This theme examines the role young people play in peacebuilding and strengthening social cohesion . It recognises that peace has both political and deeply personal dimensions. Contributions may explore experiences involving: Youth-led peacebuilding; Community reconciliation; Social cohesion; Repairing fractured relationships; Conflict transformation; Freedom; and Everyday practices that contribute to peace. The organisers welcome work that examines both large-scale political realities and the everyday experiences through which fractured communities seek repair. Theme 5: Communities of Care — Youth-Led Networks Built on Solidarity, Not Charity The fifth theme focuses on mutual aid and community solidarity . The anthology seeks contributions that demonstrate the distinction between mutual aid and conventional charitable giving. The central editorial perspective is community over individuality . Applicants could examine how young people are developing structures and networks of care that: Prioritise solidarity; Strengthen communities; Share resources; Support collective wellbeing; Build reciprocal relationships; and Avoid reproducing dependency. This theme is particularly relevant to young people working within community networks and grassroots initiatives where care is understood as a collective responsibility. Theme 6: Stories That Move Systems — Art, Culture and Storytelling as Tools for Transformation The final theme explores the role of art, culture, narrative and storytelling in systems change . The organisers are seeking contributions showing how creative practices can actively shape transformation rather than simply illustrate social issues. Relevant work could involve: Visual art; Cultural practice; Storytelling; Film; Performance; Literature; Community narratives; Creative campaigns; and Other forms of cultural expression. Applicants should demonstrate how creative practice or storytelling functions as an instrument for changing systems, perspectives, narratives or relationships. What Happens If Your Abstract Is Selected? Successful applicants will move from the abstract stage into development of the full anthology. Selected authors will be invited to prepare a contribution of approximately 2,000 words . Importantly, authors will not be expected to navigate the development process alone. The project s editorial team will provide editorial support throughout the process , helping contributors develop their initial abstracts into full pieces suitable for publication. This support is particularly significant because applicants do not need previous academic publishing or professional writing experience. The intention is to enable practitioners with valuable lived experience to communicate what they have learned in a clear and accessible way. Approximately 18 Contributions Will Be Featured The anthology is expected to bring together approximately 18 contributions from young practitioners. These contributions will collectively cover the six themes and document different approaches to youth-led systems change. By bringing these experiences together in one open-access publication, the project seeks to create a record that can contribute to discussions among young people, communities, researchers, institutions, practitioners and policymakers. Planned Launch at UNESCO MOST Forum 2027 The project aims to launch the completed six-chapter anthology at the UNESCO MOST Forum 2027 . This gives selected contributors an opportunity for their experiences and perspectives to become part of a publication intended to contribute to wider conversations about social transformation and systems change. The open-access format will also help make the anthology available beyond conventional academic or institutional audiences. Important Guidance on Artificial Intelligence and LLM Use Applicants should pay close attention to the project s guidelines concerning artificial intelligence and large language models. The organisers strongly emphasise that the call is designed to uncover original thinking, creativity and authentic perspectives from young practitioners . For this reason, using AI language models to draft, substantially revise or generate sections of a submission is not advised . The organisers explain that they expect to receive a large volume of submissions. Although AI-detection tools are imperfect, editors may recognise recurring patterns in language, tone and ideas that can cause an otherwise strong submission to appear less original or inspired. According to the guidelines, submissions that appear to rely heavily on AI are therefore likely to receive a lower assessment than work produced without such use. Limited AI Uses That Are Permitted AI tools may be used for limited supporting purposes, including: Checking grammar and spelling; Formatting references; Translating source material from languages other than English; and Conducting initial literature searches, provided the information is subsequently independently verified. Applicants who use AI in their contribution are required to include an AI declaration . The declaration must identify: The AI model and version used; The purpose or purposes for which it was used; and Confirmation that relevant data and references have been independently checked and verified by the author or authors. Applicants should therefore ensure that the ideas, experiences, arguments and core writing in their submission genuinely represent their own perspective. Why Young Practitioners Should Consider This Opportunity We Are Not Waiting offers young changemakers an avenue to turn practical experience into a documented contribution to wider conversations about systems change. For young people already engaged in community organising, environmental restoration, alternative economic practices, peacebuilding, mutual aid, cultural work or other transformative initiatives, the anthology provides an opportunity to: Document lessons from practical experience; Share approaches that may be useful to other communities; Contribute original youth perspectives to systems-change discussions; Develop a full written contribution with editorial support; Become part of an open-access publication; Connect practical grassroots experience with wider policy and systems-change conversations; and Help demonstrate that young people are already creating alternatives rather than simply waiting for future solutions. The call is particularly accessible because applicants do not need formal academic credentials, professional writing experience or institutional affiliations. The We Are Not Waiting Webinar Series Alongside the anthology, the initiative has hosted a webinar series highlighting youth-led projects already modelling ethical, ecological and socially just futures. Each session has been grounded in practical action and hosted, moderated and shaped by young people. The webinar programme includes: We Are Not Waiting: Q A Webinar Building New Systems: From Regenerative Economies to Climate Justice and Circular Living The Human Side of Systems Change: Peacebuilding, Mutual Aid and Cultural Transformation Prospective applicants can use these sessions, together with the project s Q A guide, to gain a clearer understanding of the themes, process and type of contributions being sought. About The 50 Percent at the Club of Rome The 50 Percent at the Club of Rome works to position youth leadership at the centre of systems change. Its work supports and amplifies young people who are already developing and implementing transitions that established institutions may still be discussing or debating. Within We Are Not Waiting, this philosophy is reflected in the emphasis on treating young people not simply as beneficiaries or future leaders, but as active designers and practitioners of systems change in the present. About the UNESCO–MOST BRIDGES UK Hub The UNESCO–MOST BRIDGES UK Hub generates humanities-informed research from the ground up. Its approach works with inclusive knowledge systems to support social transformation and contribute to policy and practice. Through the collaboration with The 50 Percent, the initiative seeks to connect practical youth-led knowledge and lived experience with broader research, policy and systems-change discussions. How to Submit an Abstract Applicants should first carefully review the programme information and Q A guidance before preparing their abstract. The submission process can be approached as follows: Confirm that you are aged 14–35 at the time of submission. Identify which of the six themes most closely relates to your work. Choose a real initiative, project or practice in which you are genuinely engaged. Prepare an abstract of no more than 500 words . Explain the initiative and its context. Describe what makes the work different from existing approaches. Show how the proposed contribution will use concrete examples. Reflect on what you and your community have learned and how the work relates to broader systems change. Write in your own clear and accessible voice. Review the project s AI guidelines carefully. If AI has been used within the permitted parameters, include the required AI declaration. Submit the abstract through the official submission form before the deadline. Applicants aged 18 or under should remember that an adult, such as a parent, guardian or teacher, must make the submission on their behalf and provide the required contact details. Official programme information: https://the50percent.org/programmes/we-are-not-waiting/ Submit your abstract: https://airtable.com/appsPZlhB6lztA78J/pagdYt0xmDeMv4O85/form Q A guide: https://the50percent.org/news/we-are-not-waiting-a-qa-guide-to-the-youth-led-systems-change-anthology/ Application Deadline The deadline to submit an abstract for the We Are Not Waiting youth-led systems change anthology is 31 August 2026 . Interested young practitioners should allow sufficient time to prepare an original abstract of no more than 500 words, ensure it addresses the required areas and complete the submission process before the deadline. Conclusion The We Are Not Waiting 2026 call for abstracts is an opportunity for young people who are already creating change to document their experiences and bring practical youth-led solutions into wider conversations about the future of societies, economies, communities and ecosystems. Instead of asking applicants to speculate about what young people might accomplish someday, the initiative focuses on what they are already building today . Whether that work involves regenerating ecosystems, developing community-centred economies, experimenting with circular living, repairing social divisions, building networks of mutual aid or using art and storytelling to transform narratives, the anthology seeks contributions grounded in action and lived experience. With no requirement for academic credentials, institutional affiliation or professional writing experience, the call creates space for young practitioners whose knowledge has emerged directly from doing the work. Selected applicants will have the opportunity to transform their initial abstracts into approximately 2,000-word contributions with editorial support and potentially have their experiences documented in an open-access anthology planned for launch at the UNESCO MOST Forum 2027. Young changemakers aged 14–35 who are actively working within one of the six themes should review the official guidance, prepare a clear and original abstract in their own voice, and submit their work by 31 August 2026 .
